verdict: AMD's revenue jumped 36% to $7.4B on record PC chip sales and 57% growth in data-center chips, and with costs growing far more slowly than sales, operating income leapt from $36M to $806M and net income reached $709M.

segments.name: Data Center
segments.note: EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators — demand for both drove the segment up 57% YoY.

segments.name: Client
segments.note: Ryzen processors for PCs — up 68% on strong demand for the latest 'Zen 5' chips and a richer product mix.

segments.name: Gaming
segments.note: Graphics cards and console chips — down 30% YoY as semi-custom console chip sales fell.

segments.name: Embedded
segments.note: Chips built into cars, industrial gear and communications equipment (the Xilinx business) — down 3% YoY as end markets stayed mixed.

opex.name: Research & development
opex.note: Designing the next generations of CPUs, GPUs and AI accelerators.

opex.name: Marketing, general & administrative
opex.note: Selling products and running the company.

opex.name: Amortization of intangibles
opex.note: Writing down the value of technology bought in acquisitions (Xilinx above all) — a bookkeeping charge, not cash.

otherDetail: Other income of $39M, plus $7M of equity income, less $20M of interest expense — a net +$26M.

takeaways.title: Data Center carried the growth
takeaways.text: Data Center revenue rose 57% YoY to $3.7B — half of everything AMD sells — on EPYC server processors and Instinct AI accelerators.

takeaways.title: PC chips boomed too
takeaways.text: Client revenue jumped 68% to $2.3B on 'Zen 5' Ryzen demand, more than offsetting a 30% drop in Gaming as console chip sales faded.

takeaways.title: Profits finally leveraged
takeaways.text: Operating income jumped from just $36M a year ago to $806M — revenue grew 36% while costs grew far more slowly, lifting the gross margin to 50% from 47%.
